title: Lior and the Regiment
premise: In the aftermath of a civil war that officially ended twenty years ago, Mara Hartwell works as a driver and letter-reader for Edith Voss, a celebrated suffragist whose public legend rests on a version of events Mara knows to be false. When a census taker's probing questions expose gaps in Mara's carefully constructed identity, they realize the government is quietly rewriting the war's record before witnesses die or scatter. Mara must decide whether to protect Edith's myth—and the movement it sustains—or to get the true testimony of the forgotten women who actually held the line into the official archive before the victors' historians seal it shut. The book ends with Mara testifying under their own recovered name, Edith's legend cracked but her cause intact, and the record amended just as the archive doors close.
about_author: Wren Hartwell is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloging uncatalogued letters from regional suffrage chapters. They live in a river town where the old courthouse still smells of coal smoke, and they write about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. A routine census interview turns sharp when the taker asks where Mara was in the war years—a question Mara has dodged for two decades. Mara deflects, but the taker writes something down anyway. Emotional beat: the first crack in twenty years of practiced invisibility.

chapters.title: Letters Before Delivery
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. We learn Mara's trade: driving Edith Voss to rallies and reading her correspondence aloud, editing dangerous passages by habit. A letter arrives from a historian's office requesting Edith's war papers. Beat: Mara recognizes the census taker's handwriting on the envelope.

chapters.title: The Legend of Edith Voss
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Edith rehearses her anniversary speech, the one where she stood alone at the bridge and stopped the regiment. She believes it, mostly. Beat: the comfort of a story told so long it has replaced the truth.

chapters.title: What the Driver Saw
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Flashback woven into present: twenty years ago, Mara drove the actual women to the bridge—three of them, not one—and watched the regiment pass without a shot fired because of a bribed captain. Beat: the weight of being the only witness left.

chapters.title: The Historian's Card
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara visits the census taker, Mr. Aldous Fen, at his lodging, pretending curiosity about the census. Fen reveals the Commission is compiling an 'authoritative history' with a deadline: the archive seals in eleven weeks. Beat: dread sharpening into purpose.

chapters.title: Edith's Drawer of Secrets
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Edith burns a letter from a woman named Cass, one of the bridge women, asking to be remembered. She keeps the ash in a drawer with her real diary. Beat: guilt dressed up as necessity.

chapters.title: The Third Woman
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara tracks down Cass Okafor, now a laundress in the mill district, who refuses to talk: 'The record is theirs. Why hand them more of us?' Beat: Mara learns the cost of being written down.

chapters.title: A Ride to the Coast
chapters.summary: Mara and Edith's shared POV, alternating. A long drive to a commemorative unveiling; small talk that is actually two people circling the same buried event. Beat: love and loyalty strained by what each knows the other is hiding.

chapters.title: Fen's File on Mara
chapters.summary: Fen's POV. Fen is not a mere census taker but a Commission field agent compiling 'inconsistency reports.' He has Mara's original registration from the war—the one with a name Mara abandoned. Beat: menace arriving through paperwork.

chapters.title: The Name I Gave Up
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Flashback: Mara's wartime identity, the desertion charge that forced the new name, and how Edith sheltered them—binding them to her silence. Beat: understanding that Edith's protection was also a leash.

chapters.title: Petition for the Record
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara formally petitions the Commission to submit testimony, and is told testimony requires corroboration from two named witnesses. Beat: the bureaucratic wall that makes truth harder than lies.

chapters.title: Cass at the Mill Gate
chapters.summary: Cass's POV. Cass watches Mara wait outside her shift and finally speaks—not about the bridge, but about her son, who believes the legend too and would be shamed by the truth. Beat: loyalty to family versus loyalty to fact.

chapters.title: The Anniversary Speech
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Edith delivers the bridge speech to thousands; Mara, in the crowd, hears the lie land like a bell. Fen watches Mara's face. Beat: public glory as private wound.

chapters.title: An Offer from the Commission
chapters.summary: Fen's POV. Fen offers Mara immunity from the old desertion charge in exchange for a statement 'clarifying' the bridge event—in the Commission's wording. Beat: temptation wearing an official seal.

chapters.title: The Diary in the Drawer
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara, cleaning Edith's study, finds the real diary and reads the entry from the bridge day—Edith's own hand contradicting her legend, naming all three women. Beat: betrayal and relief tangled together.

chapters.title: Confrontation in the Greenhouse
chapters.summary: Edith and Mara's POV. Mara confronts Edith; Edith argues the myth funds the movement—schools, shelters, the vote itself. 'Which truth can they afford?' Beat: the book's central argument staged as an argument between people who love each other.

chapters.title: Cass Decides
chapters.summary: Cass's POV. Cass's son finds a commemorative pamphlet with his mother's name misspelled and asks why she isn't in the picture. Cass writes to Mara that night: 'I'll say it right or not at all.' Beat: grief converting to resolve.

chapters.title: The Second Witness Problem
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Two witnesses needed: Cass is one. The third bridge woman, Ruthie, is unaccounted for—last seen in a soldiers' home upriver. Beat: a road ahead and a clock ticking.

chapters.title: Fen Closes In
chapters.summary: Fen's POV. Fen interviews Edith, politely, and lets slip that he knows about the diary's existence. Edith realizes Mara has been talking. Beat: the alliance between driver and lady cracking under surveillance.

chapters.title: The Upriver Journey
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara and Cass travel to the soldiers' home, navigating checkpoints and a Commission clerk who photographs everyone entering. Beat: two women who once stood on a bridge now sneaking toward a different kind of stand.

chapters.title: Ruthie, Quiet as Snow
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. Ruthie has not spoken of the war since; the home's routine is her armor. She recognizes Cass before Cass speaks. Beat: recognition as resurrection—Ruthie's first full sentence in years is Cass's real name.

chapters.title: What Ruthie Remembers
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. Ruthie's testimony: it was the bribed captain, yes, but also Ruthie herself who carried the message through the regiment's lines while Edith's part was smaller and later. Beat: the legend dismantled piece by piece by the gentlest witness.

chapters.title: Edith Reads the Petition
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. A newspaper prints news of the testimony petition naming Edith's 'companions.' Edith drafts a public denial, then cannot sign it. Beat: the moment a myth-maker meets her own reflection.

chapters.title: The Bribe's Other Side
chapters.summary: Fen's POV. Fen locates the dead captain's widow, who holds the ledger proving the bribe—and wants something in return: her husband's name kept out. Beat: even the enemy's family is bargaining with truth.

chapters.title: Mara's Arrest Warrant
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Fen, pressured by superiors who prefer the legend intact, revives the desertion charge. Mara has forty-eight hours before arrest. Beat: the cost of visibility arriving all at once.

chapters.title: Edith's Choice
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Edith can denounce Mara and save the movement's funding, or stand with the driver who knows too much. She burns the denial draft and instead writes a statement of support. Beat: love against duty, finally on the page.

chapters.title: The Widow's Ledger
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara trades the widow a promise—her husband's motive, not his name—and receives the ledger page. Beat: truth negotiated, not pure, and better for it.

chapters.title: Fen's Doubt
chapters.summary: Fen's POV. Fen rereads his own 'inconsistency reports' and realizes he has been compiling evidence of heroism, not fraud. His superior orders the archive sealed early—nine days. Beat: the instrument of erasure beginning to malfunction.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Hearing
chapters.summary: Mara, Cass, Ruthie, and Edith's alternating POVs, short sections. Four women in one kitchen, the ledger on the table, tea going cold. Beat: belonging—the family none of them planned.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara testifies under their original name, restored at last, presenting the diary, the ledger, and their own account. The Commission chair interrupts; Fen, unexpectedly, authenticates the documents. Beat: climax—the self buried for twenty years spoken aloud in an official room.

chapters.title: Edith Takes the Stand
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Edith corrects the record herself: three women, a smaller role, a shared act. She loses the anniversary legend but keeps the meaning. Beat: the legend sacrificed to save the truth it was guarding.

chapters.title: Ruthie Speaks in Open Room
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. Ruthie testifies last, slowly, and the room waits without rushing her. Her words enter the record verbatim. Beat: the quietest voice becoming the permanent one.

chapters.title: The Sealing
chapters.summary: Fen's POV. Fen files the amended record minutes before the archive seals, then resigns. Beat: the bureaucrat choosing the archive's purpose over its politics.

chapters.title: What the Papers Say
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The press spins the scandal; Edith's funding wavers; the movement fractures and then, surprisingly, reorganizes around the amended story—ordinary women, plural. Beat: truth costs, but pays differently.

chapters.title: Cass's Son Reads the Record
chapters.summary: Cass's POV. Cass takes her son to the archive and shows him his mother's name, spelled right, in the official account. Beat: inheritance repaired.

chapters.title: The Desertion Charge, Dropped
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The old charge is formally dismissed; Mara is offered Edith's old podium and declines it, keeping the driver's seat. Beat: belonging chosen over fame.

chapters.title: Edith and Mara, the Long Road
chapters.summary: Shared POV. Edith and Mara drive the coast road, the way they did before everything, and finally say the things the greenhouse argument left unsaid. Beat: love that survived the truth.

chapters.title: The Census, Corrected
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The next census comes; Mara answers every question, including where they were during the war. The taker is a young woman with Fen's old field manual. Beat: full-circle visibility, unafraid.

chapters.title: Letters After Delivery
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara still reads Edith's letters—but now reads them aloud unedited, and Edith signs her own contradictions. Beat: trust as the final amendment.

chapters.title: The Record Remains
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV, closing. Years later, Ruthie visits the archive, finds the page with three names, and touches the glass. The record holds. Beat: resolution—belonging not in legend, but in the permanent, imperfect truth.
